planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions once soil has warmed in spring, in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil; mulch heavily over winter in marginal zones to protect dormant rhizomes.

directions: This hybrid ginger lily produces large, curled, pure white flowers that resemble moths in flight, carried on dense terminal spikes from late summer into fall. The blooms release a powerful jasmine-like fragrance that carries well beyond the plant, making it a favorite for planting near patios and windows. Foliage is broad, glossy, and tropical-looking on upright unbranched canes; in zone 8-9 gardens, apply a deep mulch layer after frost knocks back the top growth to protect the rhizomes through winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil; give afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch.

directions: A lowland relative of white ginger lily, this species bears dense terminal spikes of strongly scented white flowers marked with a bright golden-yellow throat, blooming over a long summer-to-fall season. Its cane-like stems carry glossy, lance-shaped leaves typical of the butterfly ginger group. It has been grown and trialed by the Royal Horticultural Society as a garden-worthy hardy ginger, performing well where summers are warm and humid; in zone 8 gardens, cut back frosted foliage and mulch the crown heavily for winter.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Anne Bishop Ginger Lily (Apricot Hardy Ginger)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in fertile, evenly moist soil; slow to bulk up, so allow clumps several seasons to establish before dividing.

directions: A Hawaiian-bred hybrid prized for its huge, intensely sweet-scented flower heads that shift from rich golden-orange in summer heat to softer apricot-yellow as temperatures cool in fall. Sturdy canes carry the large panicles well above the foliage, making it a strong late-season focal point. It multiplies slowly compared with other hardy gingers, so established clumps are worth protecting; in zone 8-9, mulch deeply over winter since the rhizomes are only marginally hardy there.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil; among the more cold-tolerant Hedychium species and a good candidate for zone 8 borders.

directions: Native to the eastern Himalaya, this species produces dense, cylindrical spikes of fragrant orange-to-yellow, orchid-like flowers held above glossy, mid-green cane foliage in late summer and early fall. It is one of the hardier Hedychium species in cultivation, tolerating brief freezes that would kill more tender tropical gingers to the ground while the rhizome survives with mulch. Give it consistently moist, fertile soil and morning sun to light shade; divide congested clumps every few years to keep flowering strong.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizomes after soil has warmed in spring; foliage and flowers emerge quickly in summer heat, then the plant goes fully dormant in winter.

directions: A deep magenta-to-ruby-bracted selection of Siam tulip, producing the same tulip-like clustered inflorescences as the species but in a saturated wine-red tone that reads darker than the more common pink and white forms. Plants form neat clumps of narrow, upright leaves and repeat-bloom through the summer months with regular moisture and fertility. Rhizomes go completely dormant in winter; in zone 8-9, lift and store dry and frost-free, or mulch heavily in well-drained beds where winters stay mild.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in spring in rich, well-drained soil; goes fully dormant in fall and returns in mid-to-late spring.

directions: Originally sold under the name Curcuma petiolata before taxonomists sorted out the true species, this Thai introduction is grown for its broad, pleated green leaves edged in a crisp creamy-white border, giving it a hosta-like presence in shade gardens without the slug problems. Modest white flower spikes appear low in the clump in summer, but the variegated foliage is the main attraction. It spreads readily via branching rhizomes to form a dense groundcover-like patch; where winters run below zone 8, lift and store rhizomes dry over winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions with several canes attached once nighttime temperatures stay reliably warm, in a sheltered, humid spot.

directions: Jungle King is a robust, oversized selection of red ginger bearing flower heads roughly twice the size of the standard species, in the same vivid scarlet-red as classic red ginger but on taller, more vigorous canes. Small true white flowers peek out from between the densely packed bracts, which persist for weeks and are widely used in tropical cut-flower and lei work. Grow in warm, humid, wind-sheltered partial shade with rich, consistently moist soil and monthly feeding through the growing season. It has essentially no cold tolerance and is only reliably perennial in the warmest zone 10-11 gardens; elsewhere grow in a large container that can be moved under cover.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil; among the most cold-tolerant Alpinia species, useful as a shade groundcover.

directions: Native to woodlands of China, Japan, and Taiwan, this dwarf shell-ginger relative forms low, slowly spreading clumps of glossy, dark green lance-shaped leaves, topped in spring by small white flowers streaked with red. Its compact size and shade tolerance make it a useful evergreen-to-semi-evergreen groundcover under trees rather than a specimen plant. It is notably more cold-hardy than most Alpinia, with rhizomes surviving winters into the warmer parts of zone 7 under a protective mulch layer, and returning reliably each spring in zone 8-9 gardens.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in shade to part shade.

directions: This variegated sport of Japanese alpinia carries upright, glossy leaves heavily splashed with creamy white, creating a bright accent in dim woodland corners where few other gingers thrive. In spring, clumps send up short spikes of white flowers striped with red, though the foliage remains the main ornamental feature year-round. It shares its parent's unusual cold hardiness for the genus, holding foliage through mild winters and resprouting reliably from mulched rhizomes after harder freezes in zone 7b-8 gardens.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade; foliage dies back to the ground each winter.

directions: This ornamental true ginger produces tall, sculptural cone-shaped inflorescences with translucent lime-green bract bases that deepen to ruby red at the tips as the flower head matures, with small purple true flowers emerging between the bracts. The long-lasting cones make excellent cut flowers, persisting for weeks after cutting. Grow in dappled shade with steady moisture through the growing season on tall cane-like stems; the plant is deciduous, dying back with the first frost, and the rhizome survives outdoors in zone 9-11 with a heavy winter mulch, or can be lifted and stored dry where winters run colder.
